narrative:
Your application was rejected because the model predicted a 51% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it was slightly more confident you would not pass than that you would. This prediction was based on several factors, including your LSAT score of 34, which is lower than the average of 37 among students who passed, and your first- and third-year academic deciles of 3 and 1, which are far below the averages of 6 and 6 for successful students. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is actually higher than the typical 3.24 for those who passed, and your family income is lower-middle class, these strengths were not enough to overcome the other weaknesses.

Counterfactual scenarios are "what if" situations that show the smallest changes needed for the model to predict you would pass the bar exam. Out of 10 such scenarios generated, every single one required only one change: raising your LSAT score. Specifically, your LSAT needed to increase by an average of 2 points, from 34 to 36, to flip the prediction from "fail" to "pass." No other factors—like your deciles, family income, undergraduate GPA, or full-time status—changed in any scenario, meaning the model sees your LSAT score as the single most critical barrier.

This tells you that, in the model’s view, your LSAT score is the key lever for improving your chances. Your low deciles and part-time status are concerning, but the model considers them less impactful than your LSAT. To get your application approved, you would need to focus on raising your LSAT score by about 2 points, which is a realistic and achievable goal with targeted preparation. Your strong undergraduate GPA and family background are already assets, but they cannot compensate for the LSAT gap. By improving your LSAT to at least 36, you would align more closely with the profile of students who passed, making the model’s prediction shift in your favor.
